properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony's words, 2026-10-29: "There is probably some cutoff between where an agent doesn't need reflow2 because it can easily hold everything in its context and where an agent needs something like reflow2 ... if we are running something that can easily fit inside an agents context, then I'd imagine the agent might do better without reflow2, but in highly complex designs or mathematical proofs or very complex lines of reasoning, maybe not everything can fit into the context and reflow2 is necessary here ... maybe that is more the tests that we should be running of, given x amount of context, does structured (is reflow2 content) provide any benefit over unstructured set of notes? ... reflow2 is almost a two pass system. One to give it structure/order in the graph and secondly, now it can be used in a structured manner by the agent ... This may contrast with the unstructured approach of just ingesting all the notes into context and letting the agent build its own structure (which is also not visible to the human because it is internal to the model)."

MEASURED, for scale: the pilot's 60 documents are 87,588 bytes (about 22,000 tokens, roughly a tenth of a 200,000-token context); the notes-file arm's notes grew to 84,475 bytes, so its final agent held nearly the whole project at once. reflow2's own design export is 43 MB in 75,097 files (8,339 nodes, 66,755 edges): even stripped of JSON it is far larger than any context window. The pilot therefore sits in the regime Anthony predicts favours plain notes.

OPTIONS, none chosen:
(a) SIZE SWEEP: the same task at several sizes against the answering agent's context (a tenth, about equal, ten times), so the cutoff shows as a crossing of the curves.
(b) FIXED READING BUDGET: hold what the answering agent may read to the same number of tokens in every arm; notes are searched (grep) or read in part, reflow2 is queried. This isolates structure from capacity.
(c) VISIBILITY: score whether a person can trace WHY an answer is right (which records, which links) in each arm, since the notes arm's structure lives inside the model and the graph's is on the record.
(d) THE TWO PASSES COUNTED SEPARATELY: the cost of giving the content structure (the writing rounds) and the benefit of using it (the answering round), so a structure that only pays off when read many times shows as such.

PUSHBACK:
- Increment 3 (the after numbers for cues) must keep the pilot's task as it is, or before and after cannot be compared. The sweep and the budget runs are separate measurements beside it, not a change to it.
- A large synthetic corpus with a reliable key is costly to build and to check; size in (a) could come from a real design instead (a SeattleArch copy, reflow2's own design), but then the key is harder.
- (b) depends on how well the notes arm searches: grep on good notes may close much of the gap, which is itself worth knowing.

COST (a finding): (c) and (d) are small, scoring and bookkeeping on runs already planned; (b) moderate, one extra arm setup; (a) largest, mostly the corpus and its key.

properties.name: OPEN — the measurement should find the cutoff: at what size against an agent's context does reflow2 start to help, and, at a fixed amount the agent may read, does structured memory (a graph with edges) beat an unstructured set of notes?
properties.rationale: Anthony's refinement of the measurement while the pilot ran: the pilot alone cannot show where reflow2 starts to matter, because it fits in one context.
